concepts.name: What is a Polynomial? — Degree, Terms, and Standard Form
concepts.real_life_application: A chaiwala's profit over time can be modelled as 2t³ - 5t² + 3t + 10 (a cubic polynomial), where t is months. The shape of a bridge arch is a quadratic polynomial. The trajectory of a cricket ball hit by Virat Kohli is a quadratic path.
concepts.purpose: Polynomials are mathematical models that describe relationships where quantities change at varying rates. From the curve of a roller coaster to the spread of a viral reel on Instagram — they all follow polynomial patterns.
day_to_day_usage: Auto fare in Chennai: ₹25 for first km, ₹15 per km after = 15x + 10 (linear polynomial)
Area of a square plot = x² (quadratic polynomial, where x is side length)
Volume of a cylindrical water tank in a colony = πr²h = πr² × constant (quadratic in r)
Profit of a kirana shop over quarters: P(t) = 10000 + 5000t - 200t² (quadratic, shows growth then saturation)

concepts.name: Zeroes of a Polynomial — The Roots
concepts.real_life_application: A businessman wants to know when his profit becomes zero (break-even point). That's finding the zero of the profit polynomial. For P(x) = -x² + 50x - 400, solving P(x) = 0 gives the months when profit is exactly zero.
concepts.purpose: Zeroes are the 'x-intercepts' on a graph — points where the function crosses the x-axis. In real life, they represent equilibrium points: when income equals expense, when supply equals demand, when a projectile hits the ground.
day_to_day_usage: Break-even analysis: Ravi's samosa stall has profit P(x) = -x² + 40x - 300. The zeroes tell him when he neither profits nor loses.
A ball thrown upward: height h(t) = -5t² + 20t + 1. The positive zero gives when it hits the ground.
A farmer's yield Y(x) = -2x² + 60x + 200 where x is fertilizer in kg. Zeroes show when yield equals a baseline.

concepts.name: Remainder Theorem — The Shortcut for Division
concepts.real_life_application: When you want to check if a number divides another, you compute remainder. Similarly, the Remainder Theorem tells you the remainder when a polynomial is divided by (x - a) just by plugging x = a. Like checking if p(a) = 0 tells you (x-a) is a factor.
concepts.purpose: Long division of polynomials is time-consuming. The Remainder Theorem gives the remainder in seconds: just substitute the value. This is the foundation for the Factor Theorem and for understanding the behavior of polynomial functions near specific points.
day_to_day_usage: A factory owner knows production cost C(x) = 3x² + 5x + 2. To find cost at x = 10 units, just substitute: 3(100) + 50 + 2 = ₹352
Checking if a specific input gives a specific output in any polynomial model
Verifying calculations: if remainder = 0, your division (or factorization) is correct

concepts.name: Factor Theorem — Breaking Polynomials into Simpler Parts
concepts.real_life_application: Just like you break a large catering order into smaller manageable packets, the Factor Theorem breaks a cubic polynomial into three linear factors. This makes solving complex equations much simpler.
concepts.purpose: Factorization is the basis of solving higher-degree equations. If you can factor a cubic into (x - a)(x - b)(x - c), then the zeroes are simply a, b, c. This is the most common method for solving polynomial equations in board exams.
day_to_day_usage: Breaking down a 3-year business projection P(t) = t³ - 6t² + 11t - 6 into yearly factors: (t-1)(t-2)(t-3) means key events at years 1, 2, 3
Splitting a large area into smaller rectangular plots: x³ + 3x² + 2x = x(x+1)(x+2) gives dimensions

concepts.name: Relationship Between Zeroes and Coefficients
concepts.real_life_application: For a quadratic ax² + bx + c with zeroes α and β: α + β = -b/a and αβ = c/a. This means given ANY two zeroes, you can reconstruct the polynomial. A farmer who knows two critical points of his crop yield can reconstruct the entire growth model.
concepts.purpose: These relationships allow you to find zeroes without actually solving the equation — just by looking at the coefficients. They also let you verify if your factorization is correct. In higher classes, these relations extend to cubics and quartics.
day_to_day_usage: If a quadratic profit model has zeroes 5 and 10 (break-even at months 5 and 10), the polynomial is k(x² - 15x + 50) = k(x-5)(x-10)
Verifying factorization without re-expanding: check if sum of zeroes = -b/a
Quickly finding quadratic when two solutions are known in word problems

theorems.name: Remainder Theorem
theorems.statement: Let p(x) be any polynomial of degree ≥ 1, and let a be any real number. If p(x) is divided by (x - a), the remainder is p(a).
theorems.historical_context: While the concept of polynomial remainders was known earlier, Étienne Bézout (1730-1783) formally stated and proved the theorem in his 1779 work. The theorem was known in India too — the Kerala school of mathematics (14th-16th century) used similar ideas in their work on infinite series. However, Bézout's formulation is the one taught worldwide.
theorems.why_proposed: Bézout was working on solving systems of polynomial equations. He needed a systematic way to determine if a polynomial was divisible by a linear factor without performing the full division. The Remainder Theorem was a key step toward his more famous Bézout's Theorem on intersections of algebraic curves.
theorems.real_world_utility: The Remainder Theorem is used in: (1) Computer graphics — evaluating polynomial curves (Bezier curves) at specific points; (2) Numerical analysis — the Horner's method for efficient polynomial evaluation; (3) Control systems — checking if a system's characteristic equation has roots at specific values; (4) Every calculator and computer algebra system internally uses this theorem.
theorems.why_students_learn: It teaches: (1) The concept of 'substitution as evaluation' — plugging in a value gives the remainder; (2) Efficiency — a division that takes 5 minutes can be done in 5 seconds; (3) Foundation for calculus — the idea of evaluating a function near a point leads to the concept of limits and continuity; (4) Algorithmic thinking — understanding how computers evaluate polynomials efficiently.

examples.problem: Using the Remainder Theorem, find the remainder when p(x) = x³ + 3x² + 3x + 1 is divided by (x + 1).
solution_step_by_step: Step 1: Identify a: divisor is (x + 1) = (x - (-1)), so a = -1.
Step 2: By Remainder Theorem, remainder = p(-1).
Step 6: Therefore, the remainder is 0. This also means (x + 1) is a factor of p(x).

theorems.name: Factor Theorem
theorems.statement: If p(x) is a polynomial of degree ≥ 1 and a is any real number, then (x - a) is a factor of p(x) if and only if p(a) = 0. Conversely, if (x - a) is a factor, then p(a) = 0.

proposed_by.name: Étienne Bézout (formalized) / Known to earlier mathematicians
proposed_by.note: The Factor Theorem is a direct corollary of the Remainder Theorem — if remainder = p(a) = 0, then (x-a) divides exactly.

theorems.historical_context: The Factor Theorem follows directly from the Remainder Theorem. While Euclid and Arabic mathematicians knew about factoring, and the Kerala school of mathematics in India (Madhava, 14th century) used factorization in their series expansions, Bézout was the first to state both theorems as a unified framework. In Indian mathematics, Bhaskara II (12th century) used similar ideas in his work Bījagaṇita.
theorems.why_proposed: Bézout needed a rigorous foundation for factoring polynomials. The Factor Theorem turns the problem of 'find factors' into the problem of 'find a such that p(a) = 0' — which is often easier. This is the basis of all polynomial equation solving.
theorems.real_world_utility: (1) Engineering design — breaking complex polynomial models into simple factors; (2) Signal processing — factoring transfer functions to understand system behavior; (3) Computer science — polynomial-time algorithms rely on efficient factorization; (4) Machine learning — polynomial regression models use factorized forms for efficient computation.
theorems.why_students_learn: It teaches: (1) The deep connection between zeroes and factors — solving p(x) = 0 is the same as finding factors; (2) Systematic problem-solving — try values that divide the constant term to find factors; (3) The concept of 'if and only if' — a bidirectional logical relationship; (4) It's the entry point to Galois Theory in higher mathematics.

examples.problem: Use the Factor Theorem to determine whether (x - 2) is a factor of p(x) = x³ - 4x² + x + 6.
solution_step_by_step: Step 1: By Factor Theorem, (x - 2) is a factor if p(2) = 0.
Step 5: Since p(2) = 0, (x - 2) IS a factor of p(x).

examples.problem: Factorize x³ - 3x² - 9x - 5 using the Factor Theorem.
solution_step_by_step: Step 4: Factorize x² - 4x - 5: find two numbers with sum -4, product -5 → -5 and +1.

worked_examples.problem: Find the remainder when x³ + 3x² + 3x + 1 is divided by (x - 1/2).
board_mode: Step 1: By Remainder Theorem, remainder = p(1/2)
worked_examples.speed_mode: Convert everything to denominator 8: 1/8 + 6/8 + 12/8 + 8/8 = 27/8. Quick mental calculation: 1/8 + 0.75 + 1.5 + 1 = 3.375 = 27/8.
worked_examples.competitive_shortcut: Notice x³ + 3x² + 3x + 1 = (x + 1)³ exactly. So remainder = (1/2 + 1)³ = (3/2)³ = 27/8. Know your algebraic identities!

board_mode: Step 1: Constant term = 2. Possible factors of 2: ±1, ±2.
Step 2: Try p(1) = 2 - 3 - 3 + 2 = -2 ≠ 0. So (x - 1) is NOT a factor.
Step 3: Try p(-1) = -2 - 3 + 3 + 2 = 0. So (x + 1) IS a factor.
Step 5: Factorize 2x² - 5x + 2: find factors of 2×2=4 that sum to -5 → -4 and -1.
worked_examples.speed_mode: Golden step: Try small integer values (±1, ±2) first. If p(1) = 0 or p(-1) = 0, you've found a factor quickly.
worked_examples.competitive_shortcut: For symmetric cubics like this (coefficients 2, -3, -3, 2), note that if p(x) = 0, then p(1/x) = 0 too (reciprocal roots). The factors are (x+1), (x-2), (2x-1).

worked_examples.problem: Find a quadratic polynomial whose zeroes are 3 and -5.
board_mode: Step 1: Sum of zeroes = α + β = 3 + (-5) = -2
Step 4: Therefore, required polynomial is p(x) = x² + 2x - 15
worked_examples.speed_mode: Golden step: The formula is p(x) = k[x² - (α+β)x + αβ]. Just plug and simplify. k can be any non-zero constant.
worked_examples.competitive_shortcut: If k is not mentioned, any multiple of the basic polynomial works. The simplest is k=1 giving x² + 2x - 15.

board_mode: Step 1: Divide leading terms: 3x³ ÷ x² = 3x. First term of quotient = 3x.
Step 3: Subtract from dividend: (3x³ + x² + 2x + 5) - (3x³ + 6x² + 3x) = -5x² - x + 5
Step 4: Divide new leading term: -5x² ÷ x² = -5. Next term = -5.
Step 7: Degree of remainder (1) < degree of divisor (2). Stop.
worked_examples.speed_mode: Golden step: Align terms by degree. If any degree is missing, add it with coefficient 0. Always check: degree(remainder) < degree(divisor).

exercise_2_1.title: Exercise 2.1 — Polynomial Basics and Zeroes
exercise_2_1.objective: Identify polynomials, their degrees, and find zeroes graphically

problems.question: Which of the following are polynomials? (i) x² + 3x + 2 (ii) x + 1/x (iii) √x + 2 (iv) 3x³ - 2x² + 5
solution: (i) x² + 3x + 2: All exponents are whole numbers → POLYNOMIAL.
(ii) x + 1/x: Contains x^(-1) → NOT a polynomial.
(iv) 3x³ - 2x² + 5: All exponents are whole numbers → POLYNOMIAL.
problems.concept_insight: For an expression to be a polynomial, every exponent of the variable must be a whole number (0, 1, 2, 3...). No negative or fractional exponents allowed.

problems.question: Find the degree of the polynomial p(x) = 5x⁴ - 3x² + 7x - 9.
solution: Step 1: Identify the highest power of x in the expression.
problems.concept_insight: The degree of a polynomial is the highest exponent of the variable. Constant term has degree 0.

problems.question: The graph of y = p(x) is given below (the graph crosses x-axis at -2, 1, and 3.5). Find the number of zeroes of p(x).
solution: Step 1: Zeroes of a polynomial are the x-coordinates where the graph intersects the x-axis.
Step 2: The graph crosses at three points: x = -2, x = 1, and x = 3.5.
Step 4: Since a polynomial of degree n can have at most n zeroes, the degree of p(x) ≥ 3.
problems.concept_insight: The number of zeroes equals the number of times the graph crosses or touches the x-axis.

problems.question: For a quadratic polynomial ax² + bx + c, what is the maximum number of zeroes it can have?
solution: Step 1: A quadratic polynomial has degree 2.
Step 2: A polynomial of degree n can have at most n real zeroes.
Step 3: Therefore, a quadratic can have at most 2 zeroes.
Step 4: It could also have 1 zero (when discriminant = 0) or 0 real zeroes (when discriminant < 0).
problems.concept_insight: Degree tells you the maximum possible number of real zeroes. A quadratic (degree 2) can have 0, 1, or 2 real zeroes.

problems.question: Verify that 2 and -3 are zeroes of p(x) = x² + x - 6.
solution: Step 1: p(2) = 2² + 2 - 6 = 4 + 2 - 6 = 0. Since p(2) = 0, x = 2 is a zero.
Step 3: Both values satisfy p(x) = 0, so both are zeroes of the polynomial.
problems.final_answer: Both 2 and -3 are zeroes of p(x) = x² + x - 6.
problems.concept_insight: To verify a zero, simply substitute the value into the polynomial. If the result is 0, it's a zero.

exercise_2_2.title: Exercise 2.2 — Remainder Theorem and Factor Theorem
exercise_2_2.objective: Apply the Remainder Theorem and Factor Theorem to find remainders and factors

problems.question: Find the remainder when x³ + 3x² + 3x + 1 is divided by x + 1.
solution: Step 1: Divisor = x + 1 = x - (-1), so a = -1.
Step 2: By Remainder Theorem, remainder = p(-1).
problems.concept_insight: Remainder = 0 means (x + 1) is a factor of x³ + 3x² + 3x + 1. Indeed, x³ + 3x² + 3x + 1 = (x + 1)³.

problems.question: Find the remainder when x³ - ax² + 6x - a is divided by (x - a).
solution: Step 1: Divisor = (x - a), so by Remainder Theorem, remainder = p(a).
problems.concept_insight: The remainder is expressed in terms of a. If a = 0, remainder = 0.

problems.question: Check whether (x - 1) is a factor of p(x) = x³ - 3x² + 4x - 2.
solution: Step 1: By Factor Theorem, (x - 1) is a factor if p(1) = 0.
Step 4: Since p(1) = 0, (x - 1) IS a factor.
problems.concept_insight: The Factor Theorem is just a special case of the Remainder Theorem where remainder = 0.

problems.question: Find the value of k if (x - 2) is a factor of p(x) = x³ + kx² - 3x + 10.
solution: Step 1: If (x - 2) is a factor, then p(2) = 0.
problems.concept_insight: When a factor is given with an unknown coefficient, use the Factor Theorem to set up an equation and solve for the unknown.

problems.question: Factorize x³ - 2x² - x + 2 using the Factor Theorem.
solution: Step 1: Constant term = 2. Possible factors to try: ±1, ±2.
Step 2: Try p(1) = 1 - 2 - 1 + 2 = 0. So (x - 1) is a factor.
Step 4: Factorize x² - x - 2: find numbers with sum -1, product -2 → -2 and +1.
problems.concept_insight: Always try small integers (±1, ±2) first when using the Factor Theorem. The constant term's factors give you the best candidates.

exercise_2_3.title: Exercise 2.3 — Relationship Between Zeroes and Coefficients
exercise_2_3.objective: Explore and apply relationships between zeroes and coefficients of polynomials

problems.question: Find the sum and product of the zeroes of p(x) = x² - 5x + 6.
solution: Step 1: For quadratic ax² + bx + c, sum = -b/a, product = c/a.
Verification: The zeroes are 2 and 3. Sum = 2 + 3 = 5 ✓, Product = 2 × 3 = 6 ✓
problems.concept_insight: The sum and product of zeroes are completely determined by the coefficients. No need to find the actual zeroes!

problems.question: Find a quadratic polynomial whose sum of zeroes is -7 and product is 12.
solution: Step 2: With sum = -7, product = 12: p(x) = k[x² - (-7)x + 12].
Verification: Zeroes are -3 and -4. Sum = -7 ✓, Product = 12 ✓
problems.concept_insight: k can be any non-zero constant. In board exams, taking k = 1 gives the simplest polynomial.

problems.question: If α and β are zeroes of x² - 3x + 2, find the value of 1/α + 1/β.
solution: Step 1: From the polynomial: sum = α + β = 3, product = αβ = 2.
problems.concept_insight: Expressions in α and β can often be evaluated using just α+β and αβ without finding the actual zeroes.

problems.question: If α and β are zeroes of x² + 5x + 6, find α²β + αβ².
solution: Verification: Zeroes are -2 and -3. α²β + αβ² = 4(-3) + (-2)(9) = -12 - 18 = -30 ✓
problems.concept_insight: Factor the expression to get it in terms of α+β and αβ before substituting values.

problems.question: Find a quadratic polynomial whose zeroes are 2 + √3 and 2 - √3.
problems.concept_insight: Conjugate pairs (a + √b and a - √b) always have a rational sum (2a) and rational product (a² - b), giving a polynomial with rational coefficients.

exercise_2_4.title: Exercise 2.4 — Polynomial Long Division
exercise_2_4.objective: Divide polynomials using the long division method

problems.question: Divide x³ - 3x² + 5x - 3 by x² - 2.
solution: Step 1: Divide leading terms: x³ ÷ x² = x.
Step 7: Degree of remainder (1) < degree of divisor (2). Stop.
problems.concept_insight: Stop dividing when the degree of the remainder is less than the degree of the divisor.

problems.question: Divide 3x² - x³ - 3x + 5 by x - 1 - x².
solution: Step 1: First arrange in standard form (descending powers).
problems.concept_insight: Always write polynomials in descending powers before dividing. Missing degrees should be added with coefficient 0.

topics.name: Graphical Representation of Polynomials
topics.concept: The graph of a linear polynomial ax + b is a straight line. A quadratic polynomial ax² + bx + c is a parabola opening upward (a > 0) or downward (a < 0). The zeroes are x-intercepts of the graph.
topics.formula: Vertex of parabola: (-b/(2a), -D/(4a)) where D = b² - 4ac. Axis of symmetry: x = -b/(2a).

examples.problem: Draw the graph of p(x) = x² - 3x - 4 and find its zeroes.
solution: Step 2: Vertex = (1.5, -6.25). Since a > 0, parabola opens upward.
Step 4: Zeroes: x² - 3x - 4 = 0 → (x - 4)(x + 1) = 0 → x = 4 or x = -1.
Step 5: Plot points: (-1,0), (0,-4), (1.5,-6.25), (4,0). Draw smooth curve through these.

topics.competitive_note: Graph-based questions are common in JEE Main. Know how to find vertex, axis of symmetry, and zeroes directly from coefficients.

topics.name: Polynomials with Given Conditions
topics.concept: If zeroes α, β, γ of a cubic polynomial ax³ + bx² + cx + d satisfy specific relations (like α + β = γ), we can use sum/product formulas to find unknown coefficients.
topics.formula: For cubic ax³ + bx² + cx + d: α+β+γ = -b/a, αβ+βγ+γα = c/a, αβγ = -d/a.

examples.problem: If α, β, γ are zeroes of x³ - 6x² + 11x - 6, find α+β+γ, αβ+βγ+γα, and αβγ.
solution: Step 1: For cubic ax³ + bx² + cx + d: a=1, b=-6, c=11, d=-6.
Verification: Zeroes are 1, 2, 3. Sum = 6, sum of products = 1×2+2×3+3×1 = 2+6+3 = 11, product = 6. ✓

topics.competitive_note: These relationships are heavily tested in JEE Main. Memorize the formulas for both quadratic and cubic.

topics.name: Division Algorithm for Polynomials
topics.concept: For any polynomials p(x) and g(x) with g(x) ≠ 0, there exist unique polynomials q(x) and r(x) such that p(x) = g(x)·q(x) + r(x), where degree(r) < degree(g). This mirrors the Euclid Division Lemma for integers.

examples.problem: Find all zeroes of 2x⁴ - 3x³ - 3x² + 6x - 2 if two zeroes are √2 and -√2.
solution: Step 1: Since √2 and -√2 are zeroes, (x-√2)(x+√2) = x² - 2 is a factor.
Step 4: Remaining zeroes: x = 1/2 and x = 1.

topics.competitive_note: When some zeroes are given, use them to form a factor, divide, and reduce the problem to a lower degree polynomial.

topics.name: Miscellaneous Word Problems on Polynomials
topics.concept: Real-world problems often translate to polynomial equations. Identify the unknown quantity as x, form the polynomial equation, and solve by factoring.

examples.problem: Ravi is 5 years older than his sister Priya. The product of their ages is 84. Find their ages.
solution: Step 1: Let Priya's age = x. Then Ravi's age = x + 5.
examples.final_answer: Priya is 7 years old, Ravi is 12 years old.

simple.question: What is the degree of the polynomial 3x⁵ - 2x³ + 7?

explanation.correct: Degree = 5, because the highest exponent of x is 5 (in term 3x⁵).

wrong_options.0: 3 is the coefficient of x⁵, not the degree
wrong_options.2: 7 is the constant term, not the degree
wrong_options.3: The term with exponent 2 doesn't exist in this polynomial

simple.question: Which of the following is a polynomial?

explanation.correct: x² + 2x + 1 has only whole number exponents (2, 1, 0) → polynomial.

wrong_options.1: 1/x = x⁻¹ has negative exponent → not a polynomial
wrong_options.2: √x = x^(1/2) has fractional exponent → not a polynomial
wrong_options.3: 2ˣ has variable in exponent → not a polynomial (it's exponential)

simple.question: What is the remainder when x² - 3x + 2 is divided by (x - 1)?

explanation.correct: By Remainder Theorem, remainder = p(1) = 1 - 3 + 2 = 0.

simple.question: If p(2) = 0 for a polynomial p(x), which of these is a factor?

explanation.correct: By Factor Theorem, if p(2) = 0, then (x - 2) is a factor. Since (2 - x) = -(x - 2), it differs only by a constant factor, so it's also considered a factor.

wrong_options.0: (x - 2) is correct but not the complete answer
wrong_options.2: (2 - x) is correct but not the complete answer

simple.question: For a quadratic ax² + bx + c, the sum of zeroes equals:

explanation.correct: Sum of zeroes = -b/a. For example, x² - 5x + 6 has zeroes 2 and 3, sum = 5 = -(-5)/1.

wrong_options.1: b/a is wrong; it's -b/a with a negative sign
wrong_options.2: -c/a is not the sum; c/a is the product of zeroes
wrong_options.3: c/a is the product, not the sum

simple.question: How many zeroes does a quadratic polynomial have at most?

explanation.correct: A quadratic polynomial has degree 2, so it can have at most 2 zeroes.

wrong_options.0: A quadratic always has at least 0 real zeroes but at most 2
wrong_options.1: It can have 1 zero (when discriminant = 0) but can also have 2
wrong_options.3: 3 zeroes would require degree 3 (cubic polynomial)

simple.question: What type of graph does a quadratic polynomial produce?

explanation.correct: A quadratic polynomial ax² + bx + c gives a parabola as its graph, opening upward if a > 0, downward if a < 0.

wrong_options.0: Straight line comes from a linear polynomial (degree 1)
wrong_options.2: Hyperbola comes from 1/x type rational functions
wrong_options.3: Circle comes from equations like x² + y² = r²

simple.question: A polynomial of degree n has at most how many zeroes?

explanation.correct: A polynomial of degree n can have at most n real zeroes. This is the Fundamental Theorem of Algebra.

complex.question: Find the value of k for which the polynomial x⁴ - 2x³ + 3x² - kx + 1 is exactly divisible by x - 1.

explanation.correct: If divisible by (x-1), then p(1) = 0. p(1) = 1 - 2 + 3 - k + 1 = 3 - k = 0 → k = 3.

flowcharts.title: How to Factorize a Cubic Polynomial

steps.action: Identify constant term. List its factors (± values).
Try each factor 'a': compute p(a). Is p(a) = 0?
(x - a) is a factor. Divide p(x) by (x - a) using synthetic/long division.
Factorize the resulting quadratic (splitting middle term or formula).
Try next factor from list. Are all factors exhausted?
The cubic may have no rational factors. Use other methods (grouping, etc.)
Identify divisor: write it in the form (x - a)
Note the value of 'a' (watch sign: x+5 = x-(-5), so a=-5)
Substitute x = a into the polynomial p(x)
p(a) is the remainder. If p(a)=0, divisor is a factor.

common_misconceptions: Any expression with x is a polynomial — FALSE: x + 1/x has x⁻¹ (negative exponent), √x has x^(1/2) (fractional exponent). Only whole number exponents allowed.
The degree of a polynomial is the number of terms — FALSE: Degree is the highest exponent, not the count of terms. x² + 1 has degree 2 but only 2 terms.
If p(a) = 0, then (x + a) is a factor — FALSE: If p(a) = 0, then (x - a) is a factor. So p(5)=0 means (x-5) is a factor, not (x+5).
The Remainder Theorem works for any divisor — FALSE: It only works for linear divisors of the form (x - a). For quadratic divisors, you need the general division algorithm.
A quadratic polynomial always has two real zeroes — FALSE: It can have 0 (discriminant < 0), 1 (discriminant = 0), or 2 (discriminant > 0) real zeroes.
The sum of zeroes of ax² + bx + c is b/a — FALSE: It is -b/a. The negative sign is crucial. x² - 5x + 6 has sum = 5 = -(-5)/1.
Synthetic division works for any divisor — FALSE: It only works for linear divisors (x - a). For quadratic or higher divisors, use long division.
If (x - a) is a factor, then p(a) = 0 is true, but the converse is also the same statement — CORRECT: Factor Theorem says both directions.
